idiom_name: owner-held cancellation source + read-only signal passed through every operation + checkpoint discipline
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one owner creates a cancellation source and keeps the only trigger; every operation that can block or loop receives a read-only signal as an explicit parameter and forwards it to its own callees. The operation checks the signal at safe points - typically once per loop iteration and around blocking calls - and on observing a request stops at that point, releases what it acquired on the way in and reports a cancelled outcome. Derive child signals for sub-operations (or use the runtime's parent/child structure) so cancelling the parent covers the subtree; link additional triggers such as deadlines into the same signal instead of overloading two mechanisms. Keep the trigger with the owner, never with the receiver.
code_sketch:
source = newCancellationSource()          # one owner holds the trigger
signal = source.token                     # read-only, passed down
result = run(signal)                      # forwards it to every callee

def run(signal):
    for chunk in work:
        if signal.cancelled():            # safe point
            cleanup(); return CANCELLED
        process(chunk, signal)           # blocking calls get the signal too

source.cancel(reason="client disconnected")  # request, not termination
pitfalls: Building the signal but never checking it: the operation runs to completion and the canceller waits for a cancellation that never lands.
Sending the request from the receiving side or from an ambient global instead of the owner, so unrelated work is cancelled and authority is unclear.
Using one long-lived signal for many operations: it is one-shot, so the first cancellation poisons every later operation that shares it.
Treating the request as forced termination - tearing down threads, aborting I/O buffers or leaving cleanup to the platform - and losing the consistency the cooperative model exists to preserve.
Propagating cancellation to external systems without confirming they received and honored it: a cancelled database call may still have committed on the server even though the client stopped waiting.

Performing irreversible side effects before a safe point then checking cancellation after: if the effect has already happened, cancellation is too late and the outcome should be treated as success, not cancellation.

Not accounting for cancellation arriving between checkpoint and actual work: if an operation checks cancellation, then acquires a resource and does work, the resource may be held longer than expected after a cancellation request.
